newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Pundits flock to vote-alike French village.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pundits flock to vote-alike French village.

text.p: Opinion pollsters and journalists are converging on a sleepy farming village in Burgundy which has voted the same way as the whole of France in national elections since 1981.

With less than two weeks to go until the first round of a snap parliamentary election called by President Jacques Chirac, the 1,322 registered voters of Donzy are under siege from pundits seeking to take the nation's pulse.

The village of 1,733 souls, nestled in farmland 200 km (125 miles) south of Paris, has become a sample, whose views on unemployment, the conditions for a single European currency or tax policy are a hot commodity for political professionals.
True to form, the Donziais, as residents are called, reflect the main trends of the moment: disenchantment, indifference and a slight, grudging preference for the centre-right coalition.
CONSERVATIVES COULD WIN POLL
Pierre Pradalier, a long-serving former mayor, reluctantly predicts a conservative win.
"When I heard the National Assembly had been dissolved, I thought the outcome would be tight, but you can't tell.
"There is a certain unhappiness with politics and with the current conservative coalition. But people don't find any great satisfaction with the opposition either," he said.
Several villagers, including shopkeepers speaking on condition of anonymity, said they planned to cast a protest vote for Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right National Front.
Donzy reflected the national vote in the 1995 presidential election down to the exact percentage point: 52.7 percent for Chirac against 47.3 percent for Socialist Lionel Jospin.
In 1981 and 1988, the town gave its votes to the late president Francois Mitterrand, a regular visitor to Donzy whose Chateau-Chinon constituency was in the same Nievre department.
SOFRES, one of France's major polling organisations, uses the first 200 ballots counted in Donzy as a key element in its election-night results projections, local officials said.

The Interior Ministry's political intelligence department, the Renseignements Generaux, often uses the little town in the Morvan hills to give the government a confidential reading of public opinion, as well as a tipoff on trends on polling day.
WHY DOES DONZY MIRROR NATIONAL TREND?
Quite why Donzy is so faithful to the national trend is a riddle, since it is not entirely typical of France's sociology.
Most people now live in cities, and farmers make up less than one million of the 57 million citizens. The local population is also older than the national average.

Apart from a big retirement home and an agricultural cooperative, there is also a factory making drinking straws, a stone quarry, a firm that makes plastic shoe heels and a small engineering workshop that makes spare parts for aircraft.
There is a block of council flats as well as a farming hamlet, half of whose population voted for Le Pen in 1995.
Unemployment is close to the 12.8 percent national rate.
Bernard Devin, 53, a left-leaning schoolteacher who is the current mayor, predicts a tight race in his constituency, which he says represents all social categories.
"This is not a village where people change their pattern of voting dramatically," he said.
"There is not a strong percentage swinging to the right or left. It is relatively stable. There is always a fraction that shifts but it's not very big," he said.
The Donziais are growing fed up with being guinea pigs for political scientists. Devin said his telephone had not stopped ringing since Chirac called the election on April 21.
Residents said they had already been interviewed by Austrian television, Radio Luxembourg and two French national channels, all in one week.

"I am sceptical," says Anne-Marie Lesort, who runs the Grand Monarque hotel and restaurant in the centre of town. "Everything we hear from our clientele does reflect a bit of France as it is today. There is a disappointment and that's unfortunate."
Broken promises, austerity, welfare reforms and record unemployment over the past two years have made Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe deeply unpopular in Donzy.
But that does not mean the left-wing opposition has won the hearts and votes of the Donziais.
"That is a mystery", said Josette Morizat, who runs a clothing shop. "I think everyone is unhappy. If everyone thinks like me, we would all cast blank ballots."
